title: HPV infection may confer slightly higher risk of new-onset heart disease and death

analysis.time: The study was published on 2026-09-02, and the findings were based on data from Swedish national registries and follow-up periods up to one year post-infection.
analysis.location_and_population: The study focused on women in Sweden, comparing those infected with HPV with uninfected controls and their unexposed full siblings.
analysis.event: A research study published in PLOS Medicine suggests that HPV infection may confer a slightly higher risk of new-onset cardiovascular disease (CVD) and death, particularly within the first year of follow-up.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The risk of new-onset CVD was 7% higher in HPV-infected women than in uninfected counterparts, with an absolute rate difference of 0.53 cases per 1,000 person-years. The risk of death was 25% higher in infected women, with an absolute rate difference of 6.71 cases per 100,000 person-years. In the first year, the risks were 43% and 86% higher for CVD and death, respectively, but declined afterward.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is observational and highlights the need for clinicians to be aware of the slightly elevated CVD risk in women with HPV, especially during the first year post-infection. The authors note that the small absolute difference means women should not be unduly concerned. The findings are based on Swedish registries and sibling comparisons, with no causally related serious adverse events recorded.

analysis.brief_en: A study published in PLOS Medicine suggests that HPV infection may slightly increase the risk of new-onset cardiovascular disease (CVD) and death in women, particularly within the first year of infection. The research, led by Karolinska Institutet, compared 497,445 HPV-infected women with 2.5 million uninfected controls and found a 7% higher risk of CVD and a 25% higher risk of death in infected women. In the first year, the risks were 43% and 86% higher, respectively, but declined afterward. The study also compared 143,787 infected women with their 174,637 unexposed siblings, yielding similar results. The authors advise clinicians to be aware of the slightly elevated CVD risk in HPV-infected women but emphasize that the small absolute difference does not warrant undue concern. No serious adverse events were recorded, and the findings are based on Swedish national registries.
analysis.summary_en: A study published in PLOS Medicine suggests that HPV infection may slightly increase the risk of new-onset cardiovascular disease (CVD) and death in women, particularly within the first year of infection. The research, led by Karolinska Institutet, compared 497,445 HPV-infected women with 2.5 million uninfected controls and found a 7% higher risk of CVD and a 25% higher risk of death in infected women. In the first year, the risks were 43% and 86% higher, respectively, but declined afterward. The study also compared 143,787 infected women with their 174,637 unexposed siblings, yielding similar results. The authors advise clinicians to be aware of the slightly elevated CVD risk in HPV-infected women but emphasize that the small absolute difference does not warrant undue concern. No serious adverse events were recorded, and the findings are based on Swedish national registries.

title: HPV vaccine uptake in US teens hasn’t increased in 4 years

analysis.time: The report states that the HPV vaccine uptake in US teens has not increased in 4 years, with data reflecting 2024 coverage. The survey data for 2025 was also mentioned, but the decline in Tdap and MenACWY was noted for 2024 compared to 2023. The publication date is 2026-09-04.
analysis.location_and_population: The report focuses on the United States, specifically on teenagers aged 13 to 17 years. It also references the broader population of US women in their 20s and the general public in Pennsylvania.
analysis.event: The event is the lack of increase in HPV vaccine uptake among US teenagers over the past four years, as reported in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. The CDC authors noted that the lower HPV vaccination coverage compared to other routine adolescent vaccines might be due to differences in school entry requirements.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In 2024, 78.2% of US teens aged 13 to 17 received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine, and 62.9% completed the series. The percentage of teens receiving both doses of the MMR vaccine was 92.5%, which is lower than the Healthy People 2030 goal of 95%. The report highlights the need for continued efforts to improve coverage, especially for HPV.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC authors suggest addressing barriers to vaccination, such as improving access to preventive care, strengthening provider communication, and increasing vaccine confidence. The report also mentions the Healthy People 2030 goals and the need for continued efforts to increase vaccination rates.

analysis.brief_en: The report highlights that HPV vaccine uptake among US teenagers aged 13 to 17 has not increased over the past four years. According to the 2025 National Immunization Survey–Teen, 78.2% of teens received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine, and 62.9% completed the series. This is lower than the Healthy People 2030 goal of 80% full vaccination. The CDC authors suggest that the lower coverage might be due to fewer states requiring HPV vaccination compared to Tdap and MenACWY vaccines. They recommend addressing barriers to vaccination, including improving access to preventive care, strengthening provider communication, and increasing vaccine confidence. The report also notes that the percentage of teens receiving both doses of the MMR vaccine was 92.5%, below the 95% Healthy People 2030 target. These findings underscore the need for continued efforts to enhance HPV vaccination rates among adolescents.
analysis.summary_en: The report highlights that HPV vaccine uptake among US teenagers aged 13 to 17 has not increased over the past four years. According to the 2025 National Immunization Survey–Teen, 78.2% of teens received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine, and 62.9% completed the series. This is lower than the Healthy People 2030 goal of 80% full vaccination. The CDC authors suggest that the lower coverage might be due to fewer states requiring HPV vaccination compared to Tdap and MenACWY vaccines. They recommend addressing barriers to vaccination, including improving access to preventive care, strengthening provider communication, and increasing vaccine confidence. The report also notes that the percentage of teens receiving both doses of the MMR vaccine was 92.5%, below the 95% Healthy People 2030 target. These findings underscore the need for continued efforts to enhance HPV vaccination rates among adolescents.
